newsitem.title: UK: Chief Rabbi fans rift among British Jews.
newsitem.headline: Chief Rabbi fans rift among British Jews.

text.p: A leaked letter from Britain's chief rabbi attacking liberal Jews inflamed bitter divisions on Friday between secular and ultra-orthodox Jews which threaten to tear Britain's Jewish community apart.

"The leaders of the Reform, Liberal and Masorti movements know that they have no enemy and opponent equal to the Chief Rabbi," Jonathan Sacks wrote to right-wing orthodox Rabbi Chanoch Padwa in a letter published by the Jewish Chronicle newspaper.

Liberal and non-observant Jews were angered when Sacks failed to attend the funeral last year of hugely popular Reform rabbi Hugo Gryn, a Holocaust survivor who promoted relations between Jews and other faiths.

But when Sacks attended a secular memorial service last month for the leading Reform rabbi, ultra-orthodox rabbis protested. His presence would be tantamount to recognising the Reform strand of Judaism which they refuse to acknowledge, they said.

"There is a sacred responsibility which rests upon me, not merely not to give this false grouping recognition, but also not to be a cause of their receiving that recognition from the state, the government and the heads of churches which is a substantive recognition in the eyes of the majority of people," Sacks wrote about progressive Jews to the head of the strict Union of Orthodox Hebrew Congregations.
The Jewish Chronicle said the letter, marked "not for publication", and written in a style of rabbinical Hebrew which it said favoured hyperbole, was leaked to it last month.
The newspaper decided to publish it because British Jews and the institution of the chief rabbi had become engulfed by a "conflict unprecedented in their history", it said.

Stopping short of joining calls for Sacks to resign, the newspaper in a leading article acknowledged that liberal Jews dismayed at his handling of the row over Gryn's funeral might be prompted to set up a leadership of their own.

The chief rabbi, who sparked another outcry in 1995 when he denounced Masorti progressive Jews as "intellectual thieves", appeared to be telling his right-wing critics that he was only publicly praising Hugo Gryn for political reasons, it added.
The crisis blew apart a facade of Jewish unity which Sacks had struggled to present to outsiders since he became chief rabbi in 1990.

Sacks, a respected writer and broadcaster outside the Jewish community, represents the mainstream traditional United Synagogue in Britain and Commonwealth countries. But he is not accepted as leader by sizeable minorities of liberal and ultra-orthodox Jews.
While pockets of orthodox Jewish revival have sprung up, religious observance among Britain's 300,000 Jews has declined and Sacks has fought to contain growing internal factions.

"I have sought to make us -- all of us -- a little prouder to be Jews," he wrote in an article next to the letter. "I have sought peace and actively pursued it...That effort has been rewarded by disdain by both sides, and now by betrayal."
